prompt: Yara, from retail operations, plans tomorrow's replenishment run and asks which store and product pairs had less than 2 weeks of stock left on 29 December 2024, at a sales rate that out-of-stock days do not pull down. Take every store and product with daily closing stock figures, and the units the store sold of that product on its own store orders (channel 'store'), each order counted on the UTC date of its order_ts, which holds UTC time. The rate window is the 28 days from 1 to 28 December 2024, both days included. An in-stock day is a day of the window whose closing stock is above 0, whatever moved the stock that day; a day with no sale counts as 0 units. A pair's weekly rate is 7 times the units it sold on its in-stock days, divided by its number of in-stock days, and its weeks of cover is its closing stock on 29 December 2024 divided by that weekly rate. Leave out a pair with no in-stock day or no units sold on its in-stock days, and keep only the pairs whose weeks of cover, before rounding, is less than 2. Return one row for each of those store and product pairs, with six columns in this order: store_id; product_id; units_on_hand, the closing stock on 29 December 2024; in_stock_days; avg_weekly_units, the weekly rate rounded to 2 decimals; and weeks_cover, worked out from the unrounded weekly rate and rounded to 1 decimal. Sort by store_id from low to high, then by product_id from low to high.
hints: Next, build one row for each store, product and day of the window from the daily stock, with the units sold that day, 0 when nothing sold.
Count a pair's in-stock days and add up their units with the closing-stock condition inside each total, then divide the stock of 29 December by the weekly rate.
why_this_works: The daily stock gives every day of the window a row, so a day with no sale counts as 0 while days with no stock drop out of the rate.
